6.1.oldText: In Africa my mother had been in the habit of bringing cakes, bread and wine to the churches built in memory of the saints. Once, when she did this, the doorkeeper stopped her. As soon as she learned that the bishop had forbidden it, she accepted his wish so devoutly and obediently that I myself was amazed at how readily she found fault with her own custom rather than argue about his ban. For no craving for wine laid siege to her spirit, and no love of wine goaded her into hating the truth, as it does to a great many men and women, who are sickened by any call to sobriety the way drunkards are sickened by a drink mixed with water. When she brought her basket of the customary festival food, to be tasted first by herself and then given away, she never set out more than one small cup of wine, diluted to suit her own very sober palate, from which she would take a sip for courtesy's sake. And if there were many shrines of the departed saints that seemed to deserve this kind of honor, she carried the same single cup around to set down at each. By then it was not only thoroughly watered but also unpleasantly lukewarm, and she would share it in tiny sips with those around her, because what she sought there was devotion, not pleasure. So when she discovered that this famous preacher and most devout bishop had ordered that it should not be done, even by those who did it soberly, so that no opening for gorging might be given to drunkards, and because these quasi-memorial feasts for the dead closely resembled the superstition of the pagans, she gave it up most willingly. In place of a basket full of the fruits of the earth, she had learned to bring to the shrines of the martyrs a heart full of purer prayers, and to give what she could to the poor. In this way the communion of the Lord's Body could be rightly celebrated in the place where the martyrs, in imitation of His Passion, were sacrificed and crowned. And yet it seems to me, O Lord my God, and this is how my heart judges it in Your sight, that perhaps she would not so easily have given up this custom if it had been forbidden by someone else whom she did not love as she loved Ambrose. She loved him dearly for the sake of my salvation, and he loved her for her deeply religious way of life, so fervent in spirit, as she went constantly to church doing good works. Often when he saw me he would break out in praise of her, congratulating me on having such a mother. He did not know what kind of son she had in me, a son who doubted all these things and did not believe the way of life could ever be found.

1.0.oldText: You are great, O Lord, and greatly to be praised; great is Your power, and Your wisdom is infinite. And man wants to praise You — man, who is only a small particle of Your creation, who carries around with him his own mortality, the evidence of his sin, the evidence that You resist the proud. Yet man still wants to praise You; he, only a particle of Your creation. You stir us up to take delight in praising You, for You made us for Yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in You. Grant me, Lord, to know and understand which comes first — to call on You or to praise You? And again, to know You or to call on You? For how can someone call on You without knowing You? Whoever does not know You may call on You as something other than You are. Or is it rather that we call on You so that we may know You? But how shall they call on Him in whom they have not believed? And how shall they believe without a preacher? And those who seek the Lord shall praise Him, for those who seek shall find Him, and those who find shall praise Him. Let me seek You, Lord, by calling on You; and let me call on You by believing in You, for You have been preached to us. My faith, Lord, shall call on You — the faith which You have given me, with which You have breathed life into me through the Incarnation of Your Son and through the ministry of the Preacher.

1.1.oldText: And how shall I call upon my God, my God and Lord, since when I call Him, I will be calling Him into myself? What room is there within me where my God can come into me? Where can God come into me — God who made heaven and earth? Is there really, O Lord my God, anything in me that can contain You? Do heaven and earth, which You have made, and in which You have made me, contain You? Or, because nothing that exists could exist without You, does everything that exists therefore contain You? Since I too exist, why do I ask that You should enter into me, I who would not exist unless You were in me? Why? Because I have not gone down into hell, and yet You are there also. For if I go down into hell, You are there. I could not exist at all, O my God, could not exist at all, unless You were in me — or rather, unless I were in You, from whom are all things, through whom are all things, in whom are all things. Even so, Lord, even so. Where do I call You to, since I am already in You? Or from where can You enter into me? Where can I go beyond heaven and earth, so that from there my God might come into me — my God who has said, "I fill heaven and earth"?

1.2.oldText: Do heaven and earth then contain You, since You fill them? Or do You fill them and still overflow, since they do not contain You? And where do You pour out the rest of Yourself, once heaven and earth are filled? Or do You have no need to be contained by anything, You who contain all things, since what You fill You fill by containing it? For the vessels You fill do not hold You up; even if they were broken, You would not be poured out. And when You are poured out on us, You are not cast down — rather, You lift us up. You are not scattered, but gather us together. But do You who fill all things fill them with Your whole self? Or, since nothing can contain You wholly, do they contain only part of You? And do they all contain the same part at once? Or does each contain its own part, the larger more and the smaller less? Is one part of You greater, then, and another less? Or are You wholly everywhere, while nothing contains You wholly?

1.3.oldText: What are You then, my God? What, except the Lord God? For who is Lord but the Lord? Or who is God but our God? Most high, most good, most powerful, most all-powerful; most merciful, yet most just; most hidden, yet most present; most beautiful, yet most strong; stable, yet incomprehensible; unchangeable, yet changing all things; never new, never old; renewing all things, and bringing old age upon the proud, and they do not know it; always working, always at rest; gathering still, yet lacking nothing; supporting, filling, and overspreading; creating, nourishing, and bringing to maturity; seeking, yet having all things. You love without passion; You are jealous without anxiety; You repent, yet grieve not; You are angry, yet serene; You change Your works, but not Your purpose; You receive back what You find, though You never lost it; never in need, yet rejoicing in gains; never greedy, yet exacting interest. You receive more than is owed so that You may owe; and who has anything that is not Yours? You pay debts, though You owe nothing; You cancel debts, though You lose nothing. And what have I said now, my God, my life, my holy joy? Or what can anyone say when he speaks of You? Yet woe to those who keep silent about You, since even the most eloquent are mute.

1.4.oldText: Oh, that I might rest in You! Oh, that You would enter my heart and make it drunk with You, so that I might forget my miseries and embrace You, my only good! What are You to me? In Your pity, teach me to say it. Or what am I to You, that You demand my love, and if I do not give it, You are angry with me and threaten me with terrible woes? Is it then a small woe not to love You? Oh, for the sake of Your mercies, tell me, O Lord my God, what You are to me. Say to my soul, "I am your salvation." Speak, so I may hear. Behold, Lord, my heart is before You; open its ears, and say to my soul, "I am your salvation." Let me hurry after this voice, and take hold of You. Do not hide Your face from me. Let me die — so that I do not die — only let me see Your face.

1.5.oldText: The house of my soul is narrow; enlarge it, so that You may enter in. It is in ruins; repair it. It has within it things that must offend Your eyes; I confess and know it. But who shall cleanse it? Or to whom should I cry out, if not You? Lord, cleanse me from my secret faults, and spare Your servant from the power of the enemy. I believe, and therefore I speak. Lord, You know. Have I not confessed my transgressions against myself to You, and have You not, my God, forgiven the iniquity of my heart? I do not contend in judgment with You, who are the truth; I am afraid of deceiving myself, lest my own iniquity lie to itself. Therefore I do not contend in judgment with You; for if You, Lord, should mark iniquities, O Lord, who shall stand?

1.6.oldText: Yet allow me to speak to Your mercy, me, who am dust and ashes. Allow me to speak, since I am speaking to Your mercy, not to scornful man. You too, perhaps, despise me, yet You will return and have compassion on me. For what would I say, O Lord my God, except that I do not know where I came from into this dying life — or should I call it living death? Immediately the comforts of Your compassion took me up, as I heard (for I do not remember it myself) from the parents of my flesh, out of whose substance You once shaped me. So the comforts of woman's milk received me. For neither my mother nor my nurses filled their own breasts for me; You gave me the food of my infancy through them, according to Your design, by which You distribute Your riches through the hidden springs of all things. You also gave me the desire for no more than You gave; and to my nurses You gave the willingness to give me what You had given them. For they, with a heaven-taught affection, willingly gave me what they had in abundance from You. For this good of mine coming from them was good for them too. Actually, it was not from them but through them; for from You, O God, come all good things, and from my God comes all my well-being. This I have learned since, as You proclaim Yourself to me through these gifts of Yours, within me and without. At that time I knew only how to suck, to rest in what pleased me, and to cry at what displeased my flesh — nothing more.

1.7.oldText: Afterward I began to smile, first in sleep, then while awake; this is what I was told about myself, and I believed it, since we see the same in other infants, though I myself do not remember it. So, little by little, I became conscious of where I was, and wanted to express my wishes to those who could satisfy them, but I could not; for my wishes were within me, and they were outside me, and no sense of theirs could enter inside my spirit. So I flung my limbs around and made noises at random, making the few signs I could, and such as I could, though in truth they were very little like what I wanted. And when I was not immediately obeyed (because my wishes were harmful or unintelligible), I became indignant with my elders for not submitting to me — with people who owed me no service, for not serving me — and I avenged myself on them with tears. I have learned that infants are like this by observing them, and they, all unconsciously, have shown me better than my nurses who knew it, that I myself was like this.

1.8.oldText: And look — my infancy died long ago, and I am still alive. But You, Lord, who live forever, and in whom nothing dies: before the foundation of the worlds, and before anything that can be called "before," You are, and are God and Lord of all that You have created. In You stand fixed forever the first causes of all unstable things; and of all changeable things, the springs abide in You unchangeable; and in You live the eternal reasons of all things unreasoning and temporal. Tell me, Lord, to me, Your humble petitioner; tell me, all-pitying, to me, Your pitiable one — did my infancy follow another age of mine that died before it? Was it the time I spent in my mother's womb? For I have heard something of that, and I have myself seen women carrying children. And before that life, O God my joy, was I somewhere or someone? For this I have no one to tell me, neither father nor mother, nor the experience of others, nor my own memory. Do You mock me for asking this, and command me to praise You and acknowledge You for what I do know?

1.9.oldText: I acknowledge You, Lord of heaven and earth, and I praise You for my first beginnings of being, and for my infancy, of which I remember nothing. For You have appointed that man should learn much about himself from others, and believe much on the word of weak women. Even then I had being and life, and (at the close of my infancy) I could look for signs by which to make my sensations known to others. Where could such a being come from, except from You, Lord? Can anyone be his own maker? Or can any stream of being anywhere flow into us, pouring essence and life, except from You, O Lord, in whom essence and life are one? For You Yourself are supremely Essence and Life. For You are most high, and are not changed, and in You today does not come to an end — yet in You it does come to an end, because all such things are in You. For they would have no way to pass away unless You upheld them. And since Your years do not fail, Your years are one today. How many of our years and our fathers' years have flowed away through Your "today," and from it received the measure and the mould of such being as they had; and still others will flow away, and receive the mould of their degree of being. But You remain the same, and all the things of tomorrow, and all that is beyond, and all of yesterday, and all that is behind it, You have done today. What is it to me if someone does not understand this? Let him also rejoice and say, "What thing is this?" Let him rejoice even in that, and be content rather to discover You by not discovering, than to not discover You by discovering.

1.10.oldText: Hear, O God. Alas, for the sin of man! So man says, and You pity him; for You made him, but You did not make the sin in him. Who reminds me of the sins of my infancy? For in Your sight no one is pure from sin, not even the infant whose life is only a day long upon earth. Who reminds me? Does not every little infant, in whom I see what I do not remember in myself? What then was my sin? Was it that I clung to the breast and cried? For if I did that now for food suitable to my age, I would rightly be laughed at and reproved. What I did then deserved reproof, but since I could not understand reproof, custom and reason forbade anyone to reprove me. For these habits, when we have grown up, we root out and throw away. Now no one who prunes knowingly throws away what is good. Or was it then good, even for a while, to cry for what, if given, would cause harm? To resent bitterly that free people, one's own elders, even the very ones who gave it birth, did not serve it? That many others, wiser than it, did not obey its every whim? To do its best to strike and hurt, because commands were not obeyed — commands which would have been obeyed to its own harm? The weakness of infant limbs, not its will, is its innocence. I have seen and observed an envious baby myself; it could not yet speak, but it turned pale and looked bitterly at its foster-brother. Who does not know this? Mothers and nurses will tell you that they calm these feelings with I don't know what remedies. Is this also innocence — that when the fountain of milk is flowing abundantly, the child cannot endure a companion sharing it, even one in the direst need, whose very life depends on that milk? We deal gently with all this, not because these are not evils or only slight ones, but because they will disappear as the years go on; for, though tolerated now, the very same tendencies are utterly intolerable when found in more mature years.

1.11.oldText: You, then, O Lord my God, who gave life to my infancy, furnishing the body You gave with senses (as we can see), knitting its limbs together, ornamenting its proportions, and, for its general good and safety, implanting in it all the vital functions — You command me to praise You for these things, to confess to You, and to sing to Your name, O Most High. For You are God, Almighty and Good, even if You had done nothing but this alone, which none but You could do: You, whose Unity is the pattern of all things, who out of Your own beauty make all things beautiful, and who order all things by Your law. This age, then, Lord, of which I have no memory, which I take on the word of others and guess at from other infants I have seen, true though that guess may be — I am unwilling to count it as part of this life of mine which I live in this world. For it is hidden from me in the shadows of forgetfulness no less than the time I spent in my mother's womb. But if I was shaped in iniquity, and in sin did my mother conceive me, where, I ask You, O my God, where, Lord, or when, was I, Your servant, guiltless? But look, I pass that period by; and what have I to do now with a time of which I can recall no trace?

1.12.oldText: Passing on from infancy, I came to boyhood — or rather, boyhood came to me, displacing infancy. And yet that did not depart (for where did it go?), and yet it was no more. For I was no longer a speechless infant, but a speaking boy. This I remember; and I have observed since how I learned to speak. It was not that my elders taught me words (as they did, soon after, other learning) by any set method; but I myself, longing by cries and broken sounds and various movements of my limbs to express my thoughts, so that I might have my will — and yet unable to express all I wanted, or to whom I wanted — I practised the sounds in my memory, by the understanding which You, my God, gave me. When they named something, and as they spoke turned toward it, I saw and remembered that they called what they were pointing to by the name they uttered. And that they meant this thing and no other was clear from the motion of their body — the natural language, as it were, of all nations, expressed in facial expressions, glances of the eye, gestures of the limbs, and tones of voice, which indicate the affections of the mind as it pursues, possesses, rejects, or shuns things. So by constantly hearing words as they occurred in different sentences, I gradually gathered what they stood for; and having broken in my mouth to these signs, I thereby gave voice to my will. So I exchanged with those around me these current signs of our wills, and in this way launched deeper into the stormy intercourse of human life, yet still depending on parental authority and the command of elders.

1.13.oldText: O God my God, what miseries and mockeries I experienced when obedience to my teachers was proposed to me as proper for a boy, so that in this world I might prosper and excel in the science of language, which would serve to gain "the praise of men" and deceitful riches. Next I was put to school to get learning, in which I (poor wretch) did not know what use there was; and yet, if I was lazy at learning, I was beaten. For this was judged right by our forefathers; and many, passing through the same course before us, laid out weary paths for us, through which we were forced to pass, multiplying toil and grief upon the sons of Adam. But, Lord, we found that people called upon You, and we learned from them to think of You (according to our powers) as some great One, who, though hidden from our senses, could hear and help us. For so I began, as a boy, to pray to You, my help and refuge; and I broke the chains of my tongue to call on You, asking You, though I was small, yet with no small earnestness, that I might not be beaten at school. And when You did not hear me (not thereby giving me over to folly), my elders — yes, my very parents, who wished me no harm — mocked my stripes, which were then my great and grievous ill.

1.14.oldText: Is there, Lord, any soul so great, and cleaving to You with such intense affection — for a kind of stupidity will in a way do it; but is there anyone who, from cleaving devoutly to You, is endowed with such a great spirit that he can think as lightly of the racks and hooks and other torments (against which, throughout all lands, men call on You with extreme dread), mocking those by whom they are feared most bitterly, as our parents mocked the torments we suffered in boyhood from our masters? For we did not fear our torments less, nor prayed any less to You to escape them. And yet we sinned, by writing or reading or studying less than was required of us. For we did not lack, O Lord, memory or capacity, of which Your will had given enough for our age; but our sole delight was play, and for this we were punished by those who were doing the same thing themselves. But the idleness of grown-ups is called "business"; that of boys, being really the same, is punished by those elders; and no one feels compassion for either boys or men. For will anyone of sound judgment approve of my being beaten as a boy because, by playing ball, I made less progress in studies which I was to learn only so that, as a man, I might play even more unbecomingly? And what else did the one who beat me do? If he was defeated in some trifling discussion with a fellow-teacher, he was more bitterly jealous than I was when beaten at ball by a playfellow.

1.15.oldText: And yet I sinned in this, O Lord God, the Creator and Disposer of all things in nature — of sin the Disposer only — O Lord my God, I sinned in transgressing the commands of my parents and those of my masters. For what they, whatever their motive, wanted me to learn, I might afterward have put to good use. For I disobeyed, not because I chose something better, but from love of play, loving the pride of victory in my contests, and wanting to have my ears tickled with lying fables, so that they might itch the more. The same curiosity flashed from my eyes more and more for the shows and games of my elders. Yet those who put on these shows are held in such honor that almost everyone wants the same for their own children, and yet are quite willing that their children should be beaten, if those very games keep them from the studies by which their parents would have them rise to be the givers of such shows themselves. Look with pity, Lord, on these things, and deliver those of us who now call upon You; deliver also those who do not yet call on You, that they may call on You, and You may deliver them.

1.16.oldText: As a boy, then, I had already heard of an eternal life, promised to us through the humility of the Lord our God stooping down to our pride; and from my mother's womb, who greatly hoped in You, I was sealed with the mark of His cross and salted with His salt. You saw, Lord, how as a boy, once seized with a sudden oppression of the stomach and like one near death — You saw, my God (for You were my keeper), with what eagerness and what faith I sought the baptism of Your Christ, my God and Lord, from the loving care of my mother and Your Church, the mother of us all. Upon which the mother of my flesh, being much troubled (since, with a heart pure in Your faith, she was even more lovingly in labour for my salvation), would in eager haste have arranged for my consecration and cleansing by the health-giving sacraments, confessing You, Lord Jesus, for the remission of sins, unless I had suddenly recovered. And so, as though I would necessarily be polluted again if I lived, my cleansing was put off, because the defilements of sin, after that washing, would bring greater and more perilous guilt. I already believed at that point, and so did my mother and the whole household, except for my father. Yet he did not prevail over the power of my mother's piety in me — that, as he did not yet believe, neither should I. For it was her earnest concern that You, my God, rather than he, should be my father; and in this You helped her to prevail over her husband, whom she, the better person, obeyed, thereby also obeying You, who had so commanded.

1.17.oldText: I long to know, my God, if You are willing, for what purpose my baptism was put off at that time. Was it for my good that the rein was loosened, as it were, so that I might sin? Or was it not loosened? If not, then why does it still echo in our ears on every side, "Leave him alone, let him do as he wants, for he is not yet baptized"? But as to bodily health, no one says, "Let him be wounded worse, for he is not yet healed." How much better, then, if I had been healed at once, and if, by my friends' care and my own, my soul's recovered health had been kept safe in Your keeping, who gave it. Better truly. But how many and great waves of temptation seemed to hang over me after my boyhood! My mother foresaw them, and preferred to expose to those waves the clay from which I might afterward be moulded, rather than the very cast once it was made.

1.18.oldText: In boyhood itself, however (so much less dreaded for me than youth), I did not love study, and hated to be forced to it. Yet I was forced; and this was well done toward me, but I did not do well; for unless I had been forced, I would not have learned. But no one does well against his will, even though what he does is good. Yet neither did they do well who forced me, but what was good came to me from You, my God. For they were careless how I should employ what they forced me to learn, except to gratify the insatiable desires of a wealthy beggary and a shameful glory. But You, by whom the very hairs of our heads are numbered, used for my good the error of all who urged me to learn; and my own error, in being unwilling to learn, You used for my punishment — a fitting penalty for one so small a boy and so great a sinner. So by those who did not do well, You did well for me; and by my own sin You justly punished me. For You have commanded, and so it is, that every disordered affection should be its own punishment.

1.19.oldText: But why did I so hate Greek, which I studied as a boy? I do not yet fully know. For I loved Latin — not what my first masters, but what the so-called grammarians taught me. For those first lessons — reading, writing, and arithmetic — I thought as much a burden and a penalty as any Greek. And yet where did this come from too, if not from the sin and vanity of this life, because I was flesh, and a breath that passes away and does not come again? For those first lessons were certainly better, because more certain; by them I gained, and still keep, the power of reading what I find written, and of writing what I want; whereas in the others, I was forced to learn the wanderings of one Aeneas, forgetful of my own, and to weep for dead Dido because she killed herself for love — all the while enduring with dry eyes my own miserable self dying among these things, far from You, O God my life.

1.20.oldText: For what is more miserable than a miserable being who does not feel pity for himself, weeping for the death of Dido because of her love for Aeneas, but not weeping for his own death because of his lack of love for You, O God? You, light of my heart, You, bread of my inmost soul, You, Power who gives vigour to my mind and life to my thoughts — I did not love You. I committed fornication against You, and all around me as I fornicated thus there echoed, "Well done! well done!" for the friendship of this world is fornication against You, and "Well done! well done!" echoes on until one is ashamed not to be such a man. And for all this I did not weep — I who wept for slain Dido, "seeking by the sword a stroke and wound extreme," while I myself was seeking a worse extreme, the most extreme and lowest of Your creatures, having forsaken You, earth passing into the earth. And if I were forbidden to read all this, I was grieved that I might not read what grieved me. Madness like this is considered a higher and richer learning than that by which I learned to read and write.

1.21.oldText: But now, my God, cry out loudly in my soul; and let Your truth tell me, "Not so, not so. Far better was that first study." For, look, I would readily forget the wanderings of Aeneas and all the rest, rather than how to read and write. But over the entrance of the Grammar School is a veil drawn — true; yet this is not so much a sign of anything mysterious as a cloak for error. Let not those whom I no longer fear cry out against me while I confess to You, my God, whatever my soul wishes, and while I acquiesce in the condemnation of my evil ways so that I may love Your good ways. Let neither buyers nor sellers of grammar-learning cry out against me. For if I ask them whether it is true that Aeneas once came to Carthage, as the poet tells, the less learned will reply that they do not know, the more learned that he never did. But if I ask with what letters the name "Aeneas" is written, everyone who has learned this will answer correctly, according to the signs which men have agreed upon by convention. If, again, I should ask which could be forgotten with the least detriment to the concerns of life — reading and writing, or these poetic fictions? — who does not foresee what everyone must answer who has not wholly forgotten himself? I sinned, then, when as a boy I preferred those empty studies to the more profitable ones, or rather loved the one and hated the other. "One and one, two"; "two and two, four" — this was to me a hateful singsong. "The wooden horse lined with armed men," and "the burning of Troy," and "Creusa's shade and sad likeness" were the choice spectacles of my vanity.

1.22.oldText: Why then did I hate the Greek classics, which contain the same kind of tales? For Homer too skillfully wove such fictions, and is most sweetly vain, yet he was bitter to my boyish taste. And so, I suppose, would Virgil be to Greek children, when forced to learn him as I was forced to learn Homer. Difficulty, in truth — the difficulty of a foreign tongue — dashed all the sweetness of Greek fable with gall, as it were. For I did not understand one word of it, and to make me understand I was urged harshly with cruel threats and punishments. There was also a time (as an infant) when I knew no Latin; but this I learned without fear or suffering, by simple observation, amid the caresses of my nursery and the jests of friends, smiling and playfully encouraging me. I learned this without any pressure of punishment urging me on, for my heart urged me to give birth to its thoughts, which I could only do by learning words — not from those who taught me, but from those who talked with me, in whose ears I also gave birth to whatever I conceived in thought. No doubt, then, that a free curiosity has more power in our learning these things than a fearful compulsion. Only this compulsion restrains the rovings of that freedom, through Your laws, O my God, Your laws, which reach from the master's cane to the martyr's trials, able to temper for us a wholesome bitter, recalling us to Yourself from that deadly pleasure which lures us away from You.

1.23.oldText: Hear, Lord, my prayer; let not my soul faint under Your discipline, nor let me faint in confessing to You all Your mercies, by which You have drawn me out of all my most evil ways, so that You might become a delight to me above all the allurements which I once pursued; that I might most entirely love You, and clasp Your hand with all my affections, and that You might still rescue me from every temptation, even to the end. For look, O Lord, my King and my God, let every useful thing my childhood learned be for Your service; for Your service let me speak, write, read, reckon. For You granted me Your discipline while I was learning vanities; and my sin of delighting in those vanities You have forgiven. Through them, indeed, I learned many a useful word, but these may as well be learned in things that are not vain; and that is the safe path for the steps of youth.

1.24.oldText: But woe to you, torrent of human custom! Who shall stand against you? How long will you not be dried up? How long will you roll the sons of Eve into that huge and hideous ocean which even those who climb the cross scarcely cross over? Did I not read in you of Jove the thunderer and adulterer? Both he could not truly be; but so the pretended thunder might give cover and pandering to real adultery. And now which of our gowned masters lends a sober ear to one from their own school who cries out, "These were Homer's fictions, transferring things human to the gods; would that he had brought down things divine to us instead!" Yet more truly could he have said, "These are indeed his fictions, but he attributed a divine nature to wicked men, so that crimes might no longer be crimes, and whoever commits them might seem to imitate not abandoned men but the celestial gods."

1.25.oldText: And yet, hellish torrent, into you are cast the sons of men with rich rewards for pursuing such learning; and a great ceremony is made of it, when this is going on in the forum, within sight of laws decreeing a salary beyond the scholars' fees. And you lash your rocks and roar, "From here words are learned; from here eloquence, most necessary for gaining your ends or maintaining your opinions." As if we would never have known such words as "golden shower," "lap," "beguile," "temples of the heavens," or others in that passage, unless Terence had brought a lewd young man onto the stage, setting up Jupiter as his example of seduction.

1.26.oldText: "Viewing a picture, where the tale was drawn, Of Jove's descending in a golden shower To Danae's lap a woman to beguile."

1.27.oldText: And then see how he excites himself to lust as if by celestial authority:

1.28.oldText: "And what God? Great Jove, Who shakes heaven's highest temples with his thunder,

1.29.oldText: And I, poor mortal man, not do the same! I did it, and with all my heart I did it."

1.30.oldText: Not one bit more easily are the words learned for all this vileness; but by means of them, vileness is committed with less shame. I do not blame the words, which are, as it were, choice and precious vessels; but the wine of error which is poured out to us in them by intoxicated teachers; and if we too do not drink, we are beaten, and have no sober judge to whom we may appeal. Yet, O my God (in whose presence I can now remember this without harm), all this I unhappily learned willingly with great delight, and for this I was pronounced a promising boy.

1.31.oldText: Bear with me, my God, while I say something about my wit, which is Your gift, and about the foolish things on which I wasted it. For a task was set me, troublesome enough to my soul, on terms of praise or shame, and fear of blows — to speak the words of Juno, as she raged and mourned that she could not

1.33.oldText: Which words I had been told that Juno never uttered; but we were forced to go astray in the footsteps of these poetic fictions, and to say in prose much of what the poet expressed in verse. And the one whose speaking was most applauded was the one in whom the passions of rage and grief were most vivid, and clothed in the most fitting language, maintaining the dignity of the character. What is it to me, O my true life, my God, that my declamation was applauded above so many of my own age and class? Is all this not smoke and wind? And was there nothing else on which to exercise my wit and tongue? Your praises, Lord, Your praises could have propped up the still-tender shoot of my heart with the support of Your Scriptures; so it would not have trailed away among these empty trifles, a defiled prey for the fowls of the air. For men sacrifice to the rebellious angels in more ways than one.

1.34.oldText: But what wonder that I was thus carried away to vanities, and went out from Your presence, O my God, when men were set before me as models who, if in relating some action of theirs — in itself not evil — they committed some barbarism or solecism, they were censured and abashed; but when in rich and adorned and well-ordered discourse they related their own disordered life, being praised for it, they gloried? You see these things, Lord, and hold Your peace; long-suffering, and plentiful in mercy and truth. Will You hold Your peace forever? Even now You are drawing out of this horrible gulf the soul that seeks You, that thirsts for Your pleasures, whose heart says to You, "I have sought Your face; Your face, Lord, will I seek." For darkened affections are what removes us from You. It is not by our feet or by change of place that men leave You or return to You. Or did that Younger Son of Yours look for horses or chariots or ships, or fly with visible wings, or journey by the motion of his limbs, that he might in a far country squander in riotous living all You had given him at his departure? A loving Father when You gave, and even more loving to him when he returned empty. So then, in lustful — that is, in darkened — affections, is the true distance from Your face.

1.35.oldText: Behold, O Lord God, yes, behold patiently, as You are accustomed, how carefully the sons of men observe the agreed rules of letters and syllables received from those who spoke before them, neglecting the eternal covenant of everlasting salvation received from You. So much so, that a teacher or learner of the inherited rules of pronunciation will offend men more by speaking, against the laws of grammar, of a "uman being" without the aspirate, than if he, being a "human being," should hate another "human being" against Your laws. As if any enemy could be more harmful than the hatred with which one is inflamed against him; or could wound more deeply the one he persecutes than he wounds his own soul by his enmity. Surely no knowledge of letters can be so deeply engrained as the record of conscience, "that he is doing to another what from another he would hate to suffer." How deep are Your ways, O God, You alone great, who sit silent on high and by an unwearied law dispense punishing blindness to lawless desires! In quest of the fame of eloquence, a man standing before a human judge, surrounded by a human throng, declaiming against his enemy with fiercest hatred, will take the greatest care lest, by a slip of the tongue, he murder the word "human being"; but takes no care that, through the fury of his spirit, he murder the actual human being.

1.36.oldText: This was the world at whose gate unhappy I lay in my boyhood; this the stage where I had feared more to commit a barbarism than, having committed one, to envy those who had not. These things I say and confess to You, my God, for which I had praise from those whom I then thought it virtue to please. For I did not see the abyss of vileness in which I was cast away from Your eyes. Before them, what more foul than I was already, displeasing even such as myself? With innumerable lies I deceived my tutor, my masters, my parents, out of love of play, eagerness to see vain shows, and restlessness to imitate them. I also committed thefts from my parents' cellar and table, enslaved by greediness, or so that I might have something to give to boys who sold me their play — which they liked no less than I did all the while. In this play, too, I often sought unfair victories, conquered myself meanwhile by the empty desire for superiority. And what could I so ill endure, or, when I detected it, rebuke so fiercely, as what I was doing to others? And when detected, if I was rebuked, I chose to quarrel rather than yield. And is this the innocence of boyhood? Not so, Lord, not so; I cry for Your mercy, my God. For these very sins, as riper years succeed, these very sins are transferred from tutors and masters, from nuts and balls and sparrows, to magistrates and kings, to gold and manors and slaves, just as severer punishments replace the cane. It was therefore the short stature of childhood which You, our King, commended as an emblem of lowliness when You said, "Of such is the kingdom of heaven."

1.37.oldText: Yet, Lord, thanks were due to You, the Creator and Governor of the universe, most excellent and most good, even if You had destined only boyhood for me. For even then I existed, I lived, and felt; and I had an implanted providence over my well-being — a trace of that mysterious Unity from which I was derived. By the inward sense I kept intact the wholeness of my senses, and in these small pursuits, and in my thoughts about small things, I learned to delight in truth; I hated to be deceived, had a vigorous memory, was gifted with speech, was soothed by friendship, avoided pain, baseness, and ignorance. In so small a creature, what was not wonderful, not admirable? But all are gifts of my God; it was not I who gave them to me; and these are good, and these together are myself. Good, then, is He that made me, and He is my good; and before Him I will exult for every good which I had as a boy. For it was my sin that not in Him, but in His creatures — in myself and others — I sought pleasures, sublimities, and truths, and so fell headlong into sorrows, confusions, and errors. Thanks be to You, my joy and my glory and my confidence, my God — thanks be to You for Your gifts; but preserve them to me. For so You will preserve me, and those things which You have given me will be enlarged and perfected, and I myself shall be with You, since even my existence You have given me.

2.0.oldText: I will now call to mind my past foulness, and the carnal corruptions of my soul — not because I love them, but so that I may love You, O my God. For the love of Your love I do it, reviewing my most wicked ways in the very bitterness of remembering, so that You may grow sweet to me (You, sweetness never failing, You, blissful and certain sweetness); gathering me again out of that dissipation in which I was torn to pieces, when, turned away from You, the One Good, I lost myself among a multiplicity of things. For in my youth I had burned long ago to be satiated with things below, and I dared to grow wild with these various and shadowy loves; my beauty wasted away, and I stank in Your eyes, while I pleased myself and was eager to please in the eyes of men.

2.1.oldText: And what did I delight in, but to love and to be loved? But I did not keep the measure of love, of mind with mind, which is friendship's bright boundary; instead, out of the muddy concupiscence of the flesh and the bubblings of youth, mists rose up that clouded and overcast my heart, so that I could not tell the clear brightness of love from the fog of lustfulness. Both boiled confusedly within me and hurried my unsteady youth over the precipice of unholy desires, and sank me in a gulf of shameful acts. Your wrath had gathered over me, and I did not know it. I had grown deaf from the clanking of the chain of my mortality — the punishment for the pride of my soul — and I strayed further from You, and You let me alone, and I was tossed about, and wasted, and dissipated, and I boiled over in my fornications, and You held Your peace, O my tardy joy! You held Your peace then, and I wandered further and further from You, into more and more fruitless seed-plots of sorrows, with a proud dejection and a restless weariness.

2.2.oldText: Oh, that someone had then tempered my disorder and put to good use the fleeting beauties of these, the outermost points of Your creation! That someone had set a limit on their pleasure, so that the tides of my youth might have cast themselves upon the shore of marriage, if they could not be calmed, and kept within the purpose of a family, as Your law prescribes, O Lord — You who this way shape the offspring of this our death, able with a gentle hand to blunt the thorns which were excluded from Your paradise. For Your omnipotence is not far from us, even when we are far from You. Otherwise I ought to have listened more watchfully to the voice from the clouds: "Nevertheless such shall have trouble in the flesh, but I spare you." And, "It is good for a man not to touch a woman." And, "He that is unmarried thinks of the things of the Lord, how he may please the Lord; but he that is married cares for the things of this world, how he may please his wife."

2.3.oldText: To these words I should have listened more attentively, and, being set apart for the kingdom of heaven's sake, should have more happily awaited Your embraces. But I, poor wretch, foamed like a troubled sea, following the rushing of my own tide, forsaking You, and I exceeded all Your limits; yet I did not escape Your scourges. For what mortal can? For You were always with me, mercifully rigorous, sprinkling with the most bitter alloy all my unlawful pleasures, so that I might seek pleasures without alloy. But where to find such pleasures, I could not discover, except in You, O Lord, who teach through sorrow, and wound us in order to heal us, and kill us so that we will not die from You. Where was I, and how far was I exiled from the delights of Your house, in that sixteenth year of the age of my flesh, when the madness of lust — to which human shamelessness gives free licence, though unlicensed by Your laws — took charge of me, and I surrendered myself wholly to it? My friends meanwhile took no care to save me from my fall by marriage; their only concern was that I should learn to speak excellently and be a persuasive orator.

2.4.oldText: For that year my studies were interrupted, while after my return from Madaura (a neighbouring city to which I had journeyed to learn grammar and rhetoric) the expenses for a further journey to Carthage were being arranged for me — arranged more by the resolution than by the means of my father, who was only a poor freeman of Thagaste. To whom am I telling this? Not to You, my God; but in Your presence to my own kind, to that small portion of mankind who may happen upon these writings of mine. And for what purpose? So that whoever reads this may think out of what depths we are to cry to You. For what is closer to Your ears than a confessing heart, and a life of faith? Who did not praise my father for providing his son with everything necessary for a far journey for the sake of his studies, beyond the capacity of his means? For many far wealthier citizens did no such thing for their children. But yet this same father had no concern for how I was growing toward You, or how chaste I was — so long as I was fluent in speech, however barren I might be toward Your cultivation, O God, the only true and good Lord of Your field, my heart.

2.5.oldText: But while in that sixteenth year I lived with my parents, leaving all schooling for a while (a season of idleness being imposed through the narrowness of my parents' fortunes), the briers of unclean desires grew rank over my head, and there was no hand to root them out. When my father saw me at the baths, now growing toward manhood, and filled with a restless youthfulness, he, already anticipating grandchildren from this, gladly told my mother, rejoicing in that tumult of the senses by which the world forgets You its Creator, and becomes enamoured of Your creature instead of You, through the fumes of that invisible wine of its self-will, turning aside and bowing down to the very basest things. But in my mother's breast You had already begun Your temple, the foundation of Your holy dwelling, whereas my father was as yet only a catechumen, and only recently one at that. She then was startled with a holy fear and trembling; and though I was not yet baptized, she feared for me those crooked ways in which those walk who turn their back to You and not their face.

2.6.oldText: Woe is me! And dare I say that You held Your peace, O my God, while I wandered further from You? Did You then indeed hold Your peace toward me? And whose, but Yours, were these words which You sang into my ears through my mother, Your faithful one? Nothing of it sank into my heart, so as to shape my actions. For she wished, and I remember how in private she anxiously warned me, "not to commit fornication, but especially never to defile another man's wife." These seemed to me womanish warnings, which I would blush to obey. But they were Yours, and I did not know it; and I thought You were silent and that it was only she who spoke — while in fact You were not silent to me through her, and it was You who, in her, were despised by me, her son, the son of Your handmaid, Your servant. But I did not know it; and I ran headlong with such blindness that among my peers I was ashamed of being less shameless when I heard them boast of their wickedness; yes, and the more they boasted, the more they were degraded; and I took pleasure not only in the pleasure of the deed but in the praise. What is worthy of dispraise but vice? But I made myself worse than I was, so that I would not be dispraised; and when in any matter I had not sinned as the abandoned ones had, I would say I had done what I had not done, so that I would not seem contemptible in proportion as I was innocent, or of less account the more chaste.

2.7.oldText: Look at the kind of companions with whom I walked the streets of Babylon, and wallowed in its mire as if in a bed of spices and precious ointments. And so that I might cling the more tightly to its very centre, the invisible enemy trampled me down and seduced me, because I was easy to seduce. Nor did the mother of my flesh — who had now fled from the centre of Babylon, though she still moved slowly in its outskirts — pay attention (as she advised me to chastity) to what she had heard about me from her husband, so as to restrain it within the bounds of married affection, if it could not be pared back to the quick. She did not heed this, for she feared a wife would prove a drag and hindrance to my prospects. Not those prospects of the world to come, which my mother placed her hopes of in You, but the prospect of learning, which both my parents were too eager for me to attain — my father, because he had next to no thought of You, and of me had only vain notions; my mother, because she reckoned that those usual courses of learning would not only be no hindrance but even some help toward attaining You. For so I conjecture, recalling as well as I can the disposition of my parents. Meanwhile the reins were slackened on me, beyond all measure of proper severity, so that I spent my time in sport, even to dissoluteness in whatever I took up. And in all of it was a mist, blocking from me, O my God, the brightness of Your truth; and my iniquity burst out as from very fatness.

2.8.oldText: Theft is punished by Your law, O Lord, and by the law written in the hearts of men, which iniquity itself does not efface. For what thief will tolerate another thief? Not even a rich thief will tolerate one who steals out of need. Yet I lusted to steal, and I did it, compelled by no hunger, no poverty, but through a satiety of well-doing and a pamperedness of iniquity. For I stole what I already had enough of, and much better than what I took. Nor did I care to enjoy what I stole; I rejoiced in the theft and the sin itself. There was a pear tree near our vineyard, loaded with fruit, tempting neither for colour nor for taste. Some lewd young fellows among us went out to shake and rob it, late one night (having, according to our pestilent custom, prolonged our sports in the streets until that hour), and took huge loads — not for our own eating, but to fling to the very pigs, having only tasted them. And this only to do what was forbidden, just because it was forbidden. Behold my heart, O God, behold my heart, which You had pity on even in the bottom of the bottomless pit. Now, behold, let my heart tell You what it sought there — that I should be gratuitously evil, having no temptation to evil except the evil itself. It was foul, and I loved it; I loved to perish, I loved my own fault — not that for which I was at fault, but the fault itself. Foul soul, falling from Your firmament to utter destruction, not seeking anything through the shame, but the shame itself!

2.9.oldText: For there is an attractiveness in beautiful bodies, in gold and silver, and all things; and in bodily touch, affinity has much influence, and each other sense has its own proper object appropriately matched. Worldly honour also has its grace, and the power of overcoming and of mastery — from which also springs the thirst for revenge. But yet, to obtain all these, we must not depart from You, O Lord, nor turn aside from Your law. The life we live here also has its own enchantment, through a certain proportion of its own, and a correspondence with all things beautiful here below. Human friendship is also endeared by a sweet tie, because of the unity formed from many souls. It is on account of all these, and the like, that sin is committed, while through an immoderate inclination toward these goods of the lowest order, the better and higher are forsaken — You, our Lord God, Your truth, and Your law. For these lower things have their delights, but not like my God who made all things; for in Him the righteous delight, and He is the joy of the upright in heart.

2.10.oldText: When, then, we ask why a crime was done, we do not believe it unless it appears that there might have been some desire of gaining one of those things we called lower goods, or a fear of losing them. For they are beautiful and comely, although compared with those higher and blessed goods they are abject and low. A man has murdered another; why? He loved his wife or his estate; or would rob for his own livelihood; or feared to lose something of this kind by him; or, wronged, was on fire to be revenged. Would anyone commit murder for no cause, delighting simply in murdering? Who would believe it? For as for that furious and savage man of whom it is said that he was gratuitously evil and cruel, yet the cause is stated: "lest" (he says) "through idleness hand or heart should grow inactive." And to what end? That through that practice of guilt he might, having taken the city, attain to honours, empire, riches, and be freed from fear of the laws, and from his troubles caused by domestic needs and the consciousness of villainies. So then, not even Catiline himself loved his own villainies, but something else for whose sake he did them.

2.11.oldText: What then did wretched I so love in you, my theft, my deed of darkness, in that sixteenth year of my age? You were not lovely, because you were theft. But are you anything, that I should speak to you like this? The pears we stole were fair, because they were Your creation, You fairest of all, Creator of all, You good God — God, the sovereign good and my true good. Those pears were fair, but it was not them that my wretched soul desired; for I had a store of better ones, and those I gathered only that I might steal. For once gathered I threw them away; my only feast in it was my own sin, which I was pleased to enjoy. For if any of those pears came into my mouth, what sweetened it was the sin. And now, O Lord my God, I inquire what it was in that theft that delighted me; and behold, it has no loveliness — I do not mean such loveliness as is in justice and wisdom, nor such as is in the mind and memory and senses and animal life of man; nor such as the stars are glorious and beautiful in their orbits; or the earth, or the sea, full of embryo-life, replacing by birth what decays; no, nor even that false and shadowy beauty which belongs to deceiving vices.

2.12.oldText: For thus pride imitates loftiness, whereas You alone are God exalted over all. Ambition — what does it seek but honours and glory? Whereas You alone are to be honoured above all, and glorious forever. The cruelty of the great wishes to be feared; but who is to be feared except God alone, from whose power what can be wrested or withdrawn — when, or where, or whither, or by whom? The tendernesses of the wanton would like to be counted as love; yet nothing is more tender than Your charity; nor is anything loved more healthfully than that truth of Yours, bright and beautiful above all. Curiosity puts on the semblance of a desire for knowledge, whereas You supremely know all. Yes, even ignorance and foolishness is cloaked under the name of simplicity and innocence, because nothing is found more single than You; and what is less injurious, since the sinner's injuries are his own works? Yes, sloth would like to be at rest; but what stable rest is there apart from the Lord? Luxury affects to be called plenty and abundance; but You are the fullness and never-failing plenty of incorruptible pleasures. Prodigality presents a shadow of generosity; but You are the most overflowing Giver of every good. Covetousness wants to possess many things; and You possess all things. Envy disputes for excellency; what is more excellent than You? Anger seeks revenge; who avenges more justly than You? Fear is startled by things unaccustomed and sudden that endanger beloved things, and takes forethought for their safety; but what is unaccustomed or sudden to You, or who separates from You what You love? Or where except with You is there unshaken safety? Grief pines for things lost, the delight of its desires, because it would have nothing taken from it, as nothing can be taken from You.

2.13.oldText: Thus the soul commits fornication when she turns from You, seeking outside You what she does not find pure and untainted until she returns to You. Thus all who remove far from You and lift themselves up against You perversely imitate You. But even by thus imitating You, they show that You are the Creator of all nature, so that there is no place whither they can retire entirely away from You. What then did I love in that theft? And in what way did I, even corruptly and perversely, imitate my Lord? Did I wish, even by stealth, to do something contrary to Your law, because by open power I could not — so that, being a prisoner, I might mimic a maimed liberty by doing with impunity things not permitted me, a darkened likeness of Your Omnipotence? Behold Your servant, fleeing from his Lord, and getting hold of a shadow. O rottenness, O monstrousness of life, and depth of death! Could I like what I was not allowed to do, only because I was not allowed to do it?

2.14.oldText: What shall I render to the Lord, that, while my memory recalls these things, my soul is not frightened by them? I will love You, O Lord, and thank You, and confess to Your name, because You have forgiven me these great and heinous deeds. To Your grace I ascribe it, and to Your mercy, that You have melted away my sins as it were ice. To Your grace I also ascribe whatever evils I have not done; for what might I not have done, I who even loved a sin for its own sake? Yes, I confess that all these things have been forgiven me — both the evils I committed by my own wilfulness and those which by Your guidance I did not commit. What man is there who, weighing his own weakness, dares to ascribe his purity and innocence to his own strength, so that he should love You the less, as though he had needed Your mercy less, by which You remit sins to those who turn to You? For whoever, called by You, followed Your voice, and avoided the things he reads me recalling and confessing about myself, let him not scorn me who, being sick, was cured by that Physician through whose aid it was that he himself was not, or was less, sick. And for this let him love You as much, or more; since by whom he sees that I have been recovered from such a deep consumption of sin, by Him he sees himself to have been preserved from the same consumption of sin.

2.15.oldText: What fruit had I then (wretched man!) in those things of which I am now ashamed to remember? Especially in that theft which I loved for the theft's sake; and it too was nothing, and therefore the more miserable was I who loved it. Yet I had not done it alone — such was I then, I remember, alone I would never have done it. I loved, then, in it also the company of the accomplices with whom I did it. So I did not love nothing else but the theft; or rather, I did love nothing else, since the circumstance of having companions was also nothing. What is it, in truth? Who can teach me, except He who enlightens my heart and uncovers its dark corners? What is it that has come into my mind to inquire about, and discuss, and consider? For had I then loved the pears I stole, and wished to enjoy them, I might have done it alone, had the bare commission of the theft been enough to satisfy my pleasure; I would not have needed to inflame the itching of my desires by the excitement of accomplices. But since my pleasure was not in those pears, it was in the offence itself, which the company of fellow-sinners produced.

2.16.oldText: What then was this feeling? For in truth it was too foul, and woe was me who had it. But still, what was it? Who can understand his own errors? It was the sport of it, which as it were tickled our hearts, that we were fooling those who little thought what we were doing, and would much dislike it. Then why was my delight of such a kind that I did not do it alone? Because people do not usually laugh alone? Ordinarily no one does; yet laughter sometimes masters men when alone and by themselves, with no one whatever with them, if anything very ludicrous presents itself to their senses or mind. Yet I had not done this alone; alone I would never have done it. Behold my God, before You, the vivid remembrance of my soul: alone, I would never have committed that theft in which what pleased me was not what I stole, but the fact that I stole; nor would I have liked to do it alone; nor would I have done it. O friendship too unfriendly! You incomprehensible ensnarer of the soul, you greediness to do mischief out of mirth and wantonness, you thirst for others' loss without any lust for my own gain or revenge — but when it is said, "Let's go, let's do it," we are ashamed not to be shameless.

2.17.oldText: Who can disentangle that twisted and intricate knot? It is foul; I hate to think of it, to look at it. But You I long for, O Righteousness and Innocence, beautiful and comely to all pure eyes, and of a satisfaction that does not cloy. With You is entire rest, and life undisturbed. Whoever enters into You enters into the joy of his Lord; and shall not fear, and shall do excellently in the All-Excellent. I sank away from You, and I wandered, O my God, too far astray from You, my support, in these days of my youth, and I became to myself a barren land.

3.0.oldText: To Carthage I came, where there sang all around me in my ears a cauldron of unholy loves. I loved not yet, yet I loved to love, and out of a deep-seated want, I hated myself for wanting not. I sought what I might love, in love with loving, and safety I hated, and a way without snares. For within me was a famine of that inward food, Thyself, my God; yet, through that famine I was not hungered; but was without all longing for incorruptible sustenance, not because filled therewith, but the more empty, the more I loathed it. For this cause my soul was sickly and full of sores, it miserably cast itself forth, desiring to be scraped by the touch of objects of sense. Yet if these had not a soul, they would not be objects of love. To love then, and to be beloved, was sweet to me; but more, when I obtained to enjoy the person I loved, I defiled, therefore, the spring of friendship with the filth of concupiscence, and I beclouded its brightness with the hell of lustfulness; and thus foul and unseemly, I would fain, through exceeding vanity, be fine and courtly. I fell headlong then into the love wherein I longed to be ensnared. My God, my Mercy, with how much gall didst Thou out of Thy great goodness besprinkle for me that sweetness? For I was both beloved, and secretly arrived at the bond of enjoying; and was with joy fettered with sorrow-bringing bonds, that I might be scourged with the iron burning rods of jealousy, and suspicions, and fears, and angers, and quarrels.

3.1.oldText: Stage-plays also carried me away, full of images of my miseries, and of fuel to my fire. Why is it, that man desires to be made sad, beholding doleful and tragical things, which yet himself would no means suffer? yet he desires as a spectator to feel sorrow at them, and this very sorrow is his pleasure. What is this but a miserable madness? for a man is the more affected with these actions, the less free he is from such affections. Howsoever, when he suffers in his own person, it uses to be styled misery: when he compassionates others, then it is mercy. But what sort of compassion is this for feigned and scenical passions? for the auditor is not called on to relieve, but only to grieve: and he applauds the actor of these fictions the more, the more he grieves. And if the calamities of those persons (whether of old times, or mere fiction) be so acted, that the spectator is not moved to tears, he goes away disgusted and criticising; but if he be moved to passion, he stays intent, and weeps for joy.

3.2.oldText: Are griefs then too loved? Verily all desire joy. Or whereas no man likes to be miserable, is he yet pleased to be merciful? which because it cannot be without passion, for this reason alone are passions loved? This also springs from that vein of friendship. But whither goes that vein? whither flows it? wherefore runs it into that torrent of pitch bubbling forth those monstrous tides of foul lustfulness, into which it is wilfully changed and transformed, being of its own will precipitated and corrupted from its heavenly clearness? Shall compassion then be put away? by no means. Be griefs then sometimes loved. But beware of uncleanness, O my soul, under the guardianship of my God, the God of our fathers, who is to be praised and exalted above all for ever, beware of uncleanness. For I have not now ceased to pity; but then in the theatres I rejoiced with lovers when they wickedly enjoyed one another, although this was imaginary only in the play. And when they lost one another, as if very compassionate, I sorrowed with them, yet had my delight in both. But now I much more pity him that rejoiceth in his wickedness, than him who is thought to suffer hardship, by missing some pernicious pleasure, and the loss of some miserable felicity. This certainly is the truer mercy, but in it grief delights not. For though he that grieves for the miserable, be commended for his office of charity; yet had he, who is genuinely compassionate, rather there were nothing for him to grieve for. For if good will be ill willed (which can never be), then may he, who truly and sincerely commiserates, wish there might be some miserable, that he might commiserate. Some sorrow may then be allowed, none loved. For thus dost Thou, O Lord God, who lovest souls far more purely than we, and hast more incorruptibly pity on them, yet are wounded with no sorrowfulness. And who is sufficient for these things?

3.3.oldText: But I, miserable, then loved to grieve, and sought out what to grieve at, when in another's and that feigned and personated misery, that acting best pleased me, and attracted me the most vehemently, which drew tears from me. What marvel that an unhappy sheep, straying from Thy flock, and impatient of Thy keeping, I became infected with a foul disease? And hence the love of griefs; not such as should sink deep into me; for I loved not to suffer, what I loved to look on; but such as upon hearing their fictions should lightly scratch the surface; upon which, as on envenomed nails, followed inflamed swelling, impostumes, and a putrefied sore. My life being such, was it life, O my God?

3.4.oldText: And Thy faithful mercy hovered over me afar. Upon how grievous iniquities consumed I myself, pursuing a sacrilegious curiosity, that having forsaken Thee, it might bring me to the treacherous abyss, and the beguiling service of devils, to whom I sacrificed my evil actions, and in all these things Thou didst scourge me! I dared even, while Thy solemnities were celebrated within the walls of Thy Church, to desire, and to compass a business deserving death for its fruits, for which Thou scourgedst me with grievous punishments, though nothing to my fault, O Thou my exceeding mercy, my God, my refuge from those terrible destroyers, among whom I wandered with a stiff neck, withdrawing further from Thee, loving mine own ways, and not Thine; loving a vagrant liberty.

3.5.oldText: Those studies also, which were accounted commendable, had a view to excelling in the courts of litigation; the more bepraised, the craftier. Such is men's blindness, glorying even in their blindness. And now I was chief in the rhetoric school, whereat I joyed proudly, and I swelled with arrogancy, though (Lord, Thou knowest) far quieter and altogether removed from the subvertings of those "Subverters" (for this ill-omened and devilish name was the very badge of gallantry) among whom I lived, with a shameless shame that I was not even as they. With them I lived, and was sometimes delighted with their friendship, whose doings I ever did abhor--i.e., their "subvertings," wherewith they wantonly persecuted the modesty of strangers, which they disturbed by a gratuitous jeering, feeding thereon their malicious birth. Nothing can be liker the very actions of devils than these. What then could they be more truly called than "Subverters"? themselves subverted and altogether perverted first, the deceiving spirits secretly deriding and seducing them, wherein themselves delight to jeer at and deceive others.

3.6.oldText: Among such as these, in that unsettled age of mine, learned I books of eloquence, wherein I desired to be eminent, out of a damnable and vainglorious end, a joy in human vanity. In the ordinary course of study, I fell upon a certain book of Cicero, whose speech almost all admire, not so his heart. This book of his contains an exhortation to philosophy, and is called "Hortensius." But this book altered my affections, and turned my prayers to Thyself O Lord; and made me have other purposes and desires. Every vain hope at once became worthless to me; and I longed with an incredibly burning desire for an immortality of wisdom, and began now to arise, that I might return to Thee. For not to sharpen my tongue (which thing I seemed to be purchasing with my mother's allowances, in that my nineteenth year, my father being dead two years before), not to sharpen my tongue did I employ that book; nor did it infuse into me its style, but its matter.

3.7.oldText: How did I burn then, my God, how did I burn to re-mount from earthly things to Thee, nor knew I what Thou wouldest do with me? For with Thee is wisdom. But the love of wisdom is in Greek called "philosophy," with which that book inflamed me. Some there be that seduce through philosophy, under a great, and smooth, and honourable name colouring and disguising their own errors: and almost all who in that and former ages were such, are in that book censured and set forth: there also is made plain that wholesome advice of Thy Spirit, by Thy good and devout servant: Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ. For in Him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily. And since at that time (Thou, O light of my heart, knowest) Apostolic Scripture was not known to me, I was delighted with that exhortation, so far only, that I was thereby strongly roused, and kindled, and inflamed to love, and seek, and obtain, and hold, and embrace not this or that sect, but wisdom itself whatever it were; and this alone checked me thus unkindled, that the name of Christ was not in it. For this name, according to Thy mercy, O Lord, this name of my Saviour Thy Son, had my tender heart, even with my mother's milk, devoutly drunk in and deeply treasured; and whatsoever was without that name, though never so learned, polished, or true, took not entire hold of me.

3.8.oldText: I resolved then to bend my mind to the holy Scriptures, that I might see what they were. But behold, I see a thing not understood by the proud, nor laid open to children, lowly in access, in its recesses lofty, and veiled with mysteries; and I was not such as could enter into it, or stoop my neck to follow its steps. For not as I now speak, did I feel when I turned to those Scriptures; but they seemed to me unworthy to be compared to the stateliness of Tully: for my swelling pride shrunk from their lowliness, nor could my sharp wit pierce the interior thereof. Yet were they such as would grow up in a little one. But I disdained to be a little one; and, swollen with pride, took myself to be a great one.

3.9.oldText: Therefore I fell among men proudly doting, exceeding carnal and prating, in whose mouths were the snares of the Devil, limed with the mixture of the syllables of Thy name, and of our Lord Jesus Christ, and of the Holy Ghost, the Paraclete, our Comforter. These names departed not out of their mouth, but so far forth as the sound only and the noise of the tongue, for the heart was void of truth. Yet they cried out "Truth, Truth," and spake much thereof to me, yet it was not in them: but they spake falsehood, not of Thee only (who truly art Truth), but even of those elements of this world, Thy creatures. And I indeed ought to have passed by even philosophers who spake truth concerning them, for love of Thee, my Father, supremely good, Beauty of all things beautiful. O Truth, Truth, how inwardly did even then the marrow of my soul pant after Thee, when they often and diversely, and in many and huge books, echoed of Thee to me, though it was but an echo? And these were the dishes wherein to me, hungering after Thee, they, instead of Thee, served up the Sun and Moon, beautiful works of Thine, but yet Thy works, not Thyself, no nor Thy first works. For Thy spiritual works are before these corporeal works, celestial though they be, and shining. But I hungered and thirsted not even after those first works of Thine, but after Thee Thyself, the Truth, in whom is no variableness, neither shadow of turning: yet they still set before me in those dishes, glittering fantasies, than which better were it to love this very sun (which is real to our sight at least), than those fantasies which by our eyes deceive our mind. Yet because I thought them to be Thee, I fed thereon; not eagerly, for Thou didst not in them taste to me as Thou art; for Thou wast not these emptinesses, nor was I nourished by them, but exhausted rather. Food in sleep shows very like our food awake; yet are not those asleep nourished by it, for they are asleep. But those were not even any way like to Thee, as Thou hast now spoken to me; for those were corporeal fantasies, false bodies, than which these true bodies, celestial or terrestrial, which with our fleshly sight we behold, are far more certain: these things the beasts and birds discern as well as we, and they are more certain than when we fancy them. And again, we do with more certainty fancy them, than by them conjecture other vaster and infinite bodies which have no being. Such empty husks was I then fed on; and was not fed. But Thou, my soul's Love, in looking for whom I fail, that I may become strong, art neither those bodies which we see, though in heaven; nor those which we see not there; for Thou hast created them, nor dost Thou account them among the chiefest of Thy works. How far then art Thou from those fantasies of mine, fantasies of bodies which altogether are not, than which the images of those bodies, which are, are far more certain, and more certain still the bodies themselves, which yet Thou art not; no, nor yet the soul, which is the life of the bodies. So then, better and more certain is the life of the bodies than the bodies. But Thou art the life of souls, the life of lives, having life in Thyself; and changest not, life of my soul.

3.10.oldText: Where then wert Thou then to me, and how far from me? Far verily was I straying from Thee, barred from the very husks of the swine, whom with husks I fed. For how much better are the fables of poets and grammarians than these snares? For verses, and poems, and "Medea flying," are more profitable truly than these men's five elements, variously disguised, answering to five dens of darkness, which have no being, yet slay the believer. For verses and poems I can turn to true food, and "Medea flying," though I did sing, I maintained not; though I heard it sung, I believed not: but those things I did believe. Woe, woe, by what steps was I brought down to the depths of hell! toiling and turmoiling through want of Truth, since I sought after Thee, my God (to Thee I confess it, who hadst mercy on me, not as yet confessing), not according to the understanding of the mind, wherein Thou willedst that I should excel the beasts, but according to the sense of the flesh. But Thou wert more inward to me than my most inward part; and higher than my highest. I lighted upon that bold woman, simple and knoweth nothing, shadowed out in Solomon, sitting at the door, and saying, Eat ye bread of secrecies willingly, and drink ye stolen waters which are sweet: she seduced me, because she found my soul dwelling abroad in the eye of my flesh, and ruminating on such food as through it I had devoured.

3.11.oldText: For other than this, that which really is I knew not; and was, as it were through sharpness of wit, persuaded to assent to foolish deceivers, when they asked me, "whence is evil?" "is God bounded by a bodily shape, and has hairs and nails?" "are they to be esteemed righteous who had many wives at once, and did kill men, and sacrifice living creatures?" At which I, in my ignorance, was much troubled, and departing from the truth, seemed to myself to be making towards it; because as yet I knew not that evil was nothing but a privation of good, until at last a thing ceases altogether to be; which how should I see, the sight of whose eyes reached only to bodies, and of my mind to a phantasm? And I knew not God to be a Spirit, not one who hath parts extended in length and breadth, or whose being was bulk; for every bulk is less in a part than in the whole: and if it be infinite, it must be less in such part as is defined by a certain space, than in its infinitude; and so is not wholly every where, as Spirit, as God. And what that should be in us, by which we were like to God, and might be rightly said to be after the image of God, I was altogether ignorant.

3.12.oldText: Nor knew I that true inward righteousness which judgeth not according to custom, but out of the most rightful law of God Almighty, whereby the ways of places and times were disposed according to those times and places; itself meantime being the same always and every where, not one thing in one place, and another in another; according to which Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob, and Moses, and David, were righteous, and all those commended by the mouth of God; but were judged unrighteous by silly men, judging out of man's judgment, and measuring by their own petty habits, the moral habits of the whole human race.
